sweep_summary: Pangasinan (pang1290) is in the catalog as lexical on Benton 1971 (Pangasinan Reference Grammar, pp. 24-26). this search of works with stress in the title had one stress-title item, Zorc 1979 'On the development of contrastive word accent: Pangasinan, a case in point' (Pacific Linguistics C-45: 241-258), already listed in the per-language bibliography and already held by the project at (open via DOI 10.15144/PL-C45.241 -> sealang.net, CC BY-SA). Read in full: it is a historical-comparative argument that Proto-Philippine penult length was lost in pre-Pangasinan and that modern Pangasinan re-developed contrastive penult and antepenult vowel length secondarily (compensatory lengthening from *qC and geminate clusters, borrowing, innovation), with a synchronic statement (p. 248, n. 2 p. 254) that modern Pangasinan has contrastive length (la:ga/laga, qanak/qa:nak, ka:ruman) and that stress is secondary to length (long vowel stressed; short penult -> ultima stress; stress shifts with intonation). classification: refines the catalog's classification - confirms lexical, adds that the contrast is phonemic vowel length (catalog length_phonemic currently null) and that antepenult accent occurs; does not supersede Benton 1971 as the deciding source. Nothing left unread; no acquisition priorities.

new_statements.quote: [p. 248] Although the original PPH length was lost in pre-Png, modern Png clearly has penult and antepenult length: la:ga 'to blanch' (#66) as opposed to laga 'to braid' (#10); qanak 'child' (#16), but qa:nak 'children' (4.2. below); ka:ruman 'yesterday' (#70). [n. 2, p. 254] Stress, taken as a primary feature of accent in Zorc (1972), is here treated as secondary to vowel length or shortness. Long vowels are generally stressed; a short penult vowel is followed by stress on the ultima (as indicated in the phonetic transcriptions given). However, stress is a syntactic feature and may shift in various sentence intonations. Vowel length is a primary feature, and is not lost.

new_statements.reading: Modern Pangasinan word accent is lexically contrastive (minimal pairs la:ga vs laga; qanak vs qa:nak), with the contrast carried by vowel length on the penult or antepenult; stress is treated as secondary and predictable from length (long vowel stressed; short penult -> ultima stress) and may shift under sentence intonation. This confirms the catalog's lexical coding (agrees with Benton 1971's láki/lakí, anák/ának pairs) and refines it: the underlying contrast is analysed as phonemic vowel length (the catalog's length_phonemic field is currently null), antepenult accent exists (ka:ruman 'yesterday', ta:wag-an), and man-/-an affixes fix length position, matching the catalog's morphology note. Zorc's paper is historical and its synchronic statement is a footnote, so it does not replace Benton's reference grammar as the deciding source.

new_statements.relation_note: Same type as the existing Zorc 1979 statement (lexically contrastive word accent). The catalog record for Pangasinan has an empty rule field; this sentence supplies the missing type (lexical/phonemic stress) but no placement detail.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is phonemic (lexically contrastive): many word pairs differ only in where the stress falls. No placement rule is given; the dictionary marks stress with an acute accent on each headword.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; only notes that conventional orthography usually leaves stress unmarked.
new_statements.identity_note: The passages read in Benton's three PALI volumes (Reference Grammar, Spoken Pangasinan, Dictionary) name no particular dialect; they describe Pangasinan as the standard language of Pangasinan province (materials based on newspapers and post-war novels per the Dictionary introduction). new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the lexical reading (inherent root stress, minimal pairs by stress) and adds the phrase-level facts (sentence-final heavy stress, alternating rhythm, rapid-speech displacement) and affix-driven shifts; it is a textbook and states no placement rule of its own.
new_statements.rule_in_words: A learner's course, not a grammar: each word has one strongly stressed syllable which is marked with an acute accent in every lesson; stress is 'inherent' to the root and some roots form minimal pairs by stress alone (ánap vs anáp, p. 157). No placement rule is stated. Speech rhythm favours alternating stressed/unstressed syllables with an extra heavy stress at the end of the sentence, and in rapid speech word stress can be displaced.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Only indirectly: 'all other syllables are, by their nature, also stressed, but to a lesser degree' (p. 621) and the even alternation of stressed and unstressed syllables (p. 12).
new_statements.exceptions: Affix-conditioned shifts: pan-..-an normally moves stress to the syllable after pan- except in roots with a stress-based minimal contrast (p. 157); man- continuous (reduplicated) forms have stress patterns depending on whether the first root syllable bears inherent stress (p. 157); sentence-final extra heavy stress and rapid-speech displacement (p. 12).

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the Zorc 1979 statement and the lexical reading (root-level contrastive stress with the same anák/ának pair) and fills the catalog's empty rule field: unpredictable primary stress on the root, rule-governed secondary stress (closed syllables, alternating rhythm), affix-driven shifts (man-, -en, -an), plural by stress shift, and phrase-final extra stress. Differs from Zorc only in analysis: Benton takes stress as the phonemic property with length a correlate ('stressed vowels may be lengthened', p. 12), whereas Zorc takes vowel length as primary and stress as predictable from it.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Every full word has one strongly stressed syllable whose position is a property of the root and is not predictable: eleven minimal pairs differing only in stress placement are listed (láki/lakí, bása/basá, óras/orás, sáli/salí, bálo/baló, tálo/taló, níman/nimán, pára/pará, ámo/amó, anák/ának, naáwat/naawát). Stress is marked with an acute accent throughout the book. Stressed vowels are tense and may be lengthened; unstressed vowels keep their quality (pp. 6, 12).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes, explicit (p. 24-25): 'syllables which end in a final consonant automatically attract a moderate stress (which we may symbolize here with a grave accent)', e.g. nátàn ‘now’; and 'there is a tendency for every alternate syllable preceding or following a strongly stressed syllable to attract medium stress, the stress pattern on a word like kabuasán /kabwasán/ ‘morning’ is thus kàbuasán, while that on mansásalita ‘is speaking’ is mansásalìta'; the two tendencies can neutralize each other (Pangasinán = pàngasinán).
new_statements.exceptions: Affixes attract or repel strong stress: man- is followed by a strongly stressed syllable (manámes vs past nanamés), -en carries moderate stress and shifts a preceding strong stress back one syllable (lútoen, amésen), -an attracts strong stress (neñgneñgán) (pp. 25, 126), with 'a few word roots which resist the demands of these affixes'; some nouns pluralize by moving stress from last to first syllable of the root (anák/ának, ogáw/agógaw, polís/popólis, p. 87); phrase-level: automatic strong stress on the syllable before a significant pause, a strong tendency to alternate weak and strong syllables, and stress displacement in connected speech (ándi báli for andí; tagá inér swamígóm) (p. 25); 'Except for the extra stress on the last syllable of the phrase, stress is placed on individual words but none is selected for major emphasis' (p. 29).
new_statements.identity_note: The passages read in Benton's three PALI volumes (Reference Grammar, Spoken Pangasinan, Dictionary) name no particular dialect; they describe Pangasinan as the standard language of Pangasinan province (materials based on newspapers and post-war novels per the Dictionary introduction). Zorc 1979 is a historical study whose synchronic statement is a footnote. Rayner 1923 (not obtained) would describe the language as of the 1920s.

readall_conflicts: No disagreement on the type or placement: all three Benton 1971 volumes and the existing Zorc 1979 statement describe Pangasinan word accent as lexically contrastive on the root (the same anák ‘child’ / ának ‘children’ pair appears in Benton's grammar p. 26/p. 87 and in Zorc). The one analytical difference is what carries the contrast: Benton calls stress phonemic and treats length as a correlate of stress ('stressed vowels may be lengthened', Reference Grammar p. 12; 'Stress is also phonemic', Dictionary p. xi), whereas Zorc 1979 (p. 248, n. 2 p. 254) takes penult/antepenult vowel length as the primary contrast with stress predictable from it. Benton additionally reports that word stress is regularly displaced in connected speech (rhythmic alternation, phrase-final extra stress, ándi báli), which Zorc's footnote also allows ('may shift under sentence intonation'). Rayner 1923 could not be opened, so it neither confirms nor contradicts.
